data.title: A small team that cooks and coaches.
data.intro: Nutriforce is a sports nutrition coaching business with its own kitchen. This is a demo business with sample content.

children.text: Who we are

The coaching side is three coaches, each working with a few sports. They write plans, run check-ins and answer messages. The kitchen has two cooks who make the weekly meals on Saturday. One coordinator handles the inbox, orders and scheduling.
Nobody on the team is listed with qualifications on this demo site. If you use this theme for a real business, add yours and any registration your country requires.
How we work
Plans are short and written in plain language. We use foods you already buy. Check-ins are by message and video, and we adjust the plan when your training changes.
We do not sell supplements, set weight targets or promise changes to your body or your performance.
About the photos

The people and food photos on this site are AI-generated illustrations. The athlete on the home page is a fictional person. She is not a member of the team, a coach or a client, and nothing on this site is her endorsement.
Medical advice

What we publish is general guidance. It does not replace advice from your doctor or a registered dietitian. If you have a medical condition, an allergy, take medication or are pregnant, speak to them before changing how you eat.

data.title: Endurance Coaching
data.summary: Food plans for runners, cyclists, swimmers and triathletes, built around your training week.

data.check_ins: Message check-in every week, video call every two weeks
data.includes:
Intro call and a review of your usual week of food
A written plan matched to your training calendar
Fuelling notes for long sessions, race day and travel
Weekly message check-in
Video call every two weeks
Optional meal prep orders at the member price

children.text: Endurance training asks a lot of your food. Long sessions need fuel on the bike or the road, hard days need a proper meal afterwards, and rest days still need to be eaten well. This plan puts those pieces on your calendar so you are not working them out at 6 am.
What we put together

After the intro call we look at your training weeks, your work hours and the food you already like. The plan is a short document: what to eat before, during and after your key sessions, a few default breakfasts and dinners, and a shopping list you can repeat.
Before an event we write a separate race-week page with meal times, what to pack and what to avoid trying for the first time on the day.
What we ask of you
Send a message once a week to say how training went and how the food worked. Tell us when something does not suit you. We adjust the plan rather than ask you to push through.
What this plan does not do

We do not promise race times, weight loss or any change to your body. We do not replace your doctor or a registered dietitian. If you have a medical condition, an eating disorder history or are pregnant, speak to your doctor first and tell us what they advise.

data.title: Strength Coaching

data.format: Daily targets set from your training split, a plain meal template, and a weekly shopping list you can batch cook from.
data.check_ins: Message check-in every week, video call every month
data.includes:
Intro call and a food diary review
Daily targets for training days and rest days
A meal template with swaps for foods you dislike
A weekly shopping list
Weekly message check-in
Video call once a month

children.text: Lifting is easier to plan around than most sports because the week is regular. Same days, same sessions. That makes the food plan simple to follow once it is written down.
How the plan is set

We ask how many days you train, how long sessions run and what your day looks like outside the gym. From that we set a protein target and a daily energy range, then split it into meals that fit your schedule.
The template lists breakfast, lunch, dinner and snack options with portions in plain terms: a palm of chicken, a fist of rice, two eggs. Swaps are built in so one dislike does not break the plan.
Check-ins
Each week you send a short message. Once a month there is a video call to review what changed in your training and adjust the targets.
What this plan does not do
We do not give training programmes. If you need one, ask your gym or a strength coach. We also do not recommend supplements or promise changes in size or weight.

data.includes:
Intro call with the player, or with the coach for a squad
Match day and training day plans
Travel and tournament food list
Weekly message check-in
A call at the start of each fixture block
Group session for squads of six or more

children.text: Team sport weeks are uneven. Two training nights, a match at the weekend, a late kick-off now and then. A good plan has to cope with that.
For individual players
We plan around your fixture list. You get a match-day timeline with what to eat and when, a lighter pattern for training nights and a few easy meals for the nights you get home late.
For squads

The group session runs for an hour at your club or on video. We cover what to eat before and after games, what to pack for away fixtures and tournaments, and how to keep a bag of food in the changing room that does not go off.
Parents and coaches are welcome on the intro call for players under 18. We ask for a parent or guardian to be on that call and to agree the plan.
What this plan does not do
We do not promise results on the pitch, and we do not advise on injury or illness. Talk to your club's medical staff or your doctor for those.

data.title: Getting Started
data.summary: A four-week starter for people new to training or coming back after a break.
data.who_for: People new to regular exercise, or returning after time away
data.sports: Walking, jogging, gym classes, home workouts
data.format: One video call a week for four weeks, a simple food plan and a shopping list. No tracking apps needed.
data.check_ins: One video call a week for four weeks
data.includes:
Intro call to talk through your week
A simple food plan with a weekly shopping list
Four weekly video calls of 20 minutes
A one-page summary at the end with next steps

children.text: If you are starting out, you do not need a spreadsheet. You need a few reliable meals, a shopping list and someone to check in with.
What happens in four weeks
Week 1: we talk through your usual week and pick two or three changes to try.
Week 2: we look at how those went and adjust the shopping list.
Week 3: we add snacks and a plan for busy days.
Week 4: we write a one-page summary of what works for you.
After the four weeks you can stop, or move to one of the ongoing plans.
What this plan does not do
We do not set weight targets or promise changes to your body. If you have a health condition or take medication, check with your doctor before changing how you eat.

data.title: What to eat before a morning run
data.excerpt: A short guide to eating before an early run, for people who do not feel like breakfast.

children.text: Early runs are awkward. You want some fuel, but a full breakfast sitting in your stomach at 6:30 is no help.
If you have an hour
Eat something small and low in fibre: a banana with a spoonful of peanut butter, or toast with honey. Drink a glass of water.
If you have twenty minutes
Go lighter still. Half a banana, a handful of dried fruit or a slice of white toast. Save the bigger breakfast for afterwards.
If you cannot eat at all
Some people run fine on an empty stomach for an easy 30 minutes. Longer or harder runs usually go better with something in you. Try a few options on easy days, never on race day.
This is general information. If you have a medical condition or take medication, ask your doctor what suits you.

data.title: Five lunches in one hour
data.excerpt: A Sunday routine for cooking a week of lunches without buying a stack of containers.

children.text: This is the routine we give most new clients. It takes about an hour and makes five lunches that do not taste the same on Friday as they did on Monday.
Cook four things
A grain: two cups of dry quinoa or rice, cooked in one pot.
A protein: chicken thighs or a tray of tofu, roasted at 200 C for 25 minutes.
A vegetable: a tray of sweet potato cubes roasted alongside the protein.
A raw side: kale or cabbage, shredded and dressed with lemon and oil.
Pack in two steps
Fill five boxes with grain and protein. Keep the raw side and any avocado in a separate tub and add them each morning, so nothing goes soft.
Boxes keep in the fridge for up to four days. For day five, freeze one box on Sunday and take it out on Thursday night.

data.title: How much protein is on your plate
data.excerpt: Rough hand-size portions for common protein foods, so you can plan without a scale.

children.text: A scale is the most accurate tool, but most people do not want to weigh food at every meal. Hand sizes are close enough to start with.
Rough numbers
A cooked chicken breast the size of your palm: about 30 g protein.
Two eggs: about 12 g.
A cup of Greek yoghurt: about 20 g.
A cup of cooked lentils: about 18 g.
These are approximate and vary by brand and cooking method.
Spread it out
Many people eat most of their protein at dinner. Moving some to breakfast is often the easiest change to make. Add eggs, yoghurt or tofu to a morning you currently spend on toast alone.
How much protein is right for you depends on your size, training and health. Your coach or a registered dietitian can help you set a figure.

data.title: Rest days are part of the plan
data.excerpt: Why we write food plans for rest days too, and what we usually put on them.

children.text: New clients often ask what to eat on days off. Many assume it should be much less. In practice we keep most things the same.
What changes
Meals are usually a little smaller, with less food built around training. A rest day still has three proper meals and some protein at each.
What stays
Sleep, water and a regular meal pattern. Rest days are a good time to batch cook, shop and plan the week ahead.
If you notice you are cutting food heavily on rest days or feel anxious about eating on them, tell your coach or speak to your doctor.

data.title: Eating the week before a first 10k
data.excerpt: What to keep the same, what to leave alone, and what to pack for race morning.

children.text: The week before your first 10k is not the time to change how you eat. Most of what you need to do is avoid new things.
Keep the same
Eat the breakfasts, lunches and dinners you have been eating on training weeks. If a meal has been working, repeat it.
Leave alone
New supplements, unfamiliar restaurants the night before and very large portions. None of these help and some upset your stomach.
Race morning
Eat what you ate before your longest training runs, about two hours before the start. Pack a banana and water in case you are waiting around. Check the event information for what the course provides.

data.title: Spinach and lemon smoothie
data.excerpt: The recipe for the smoothie on our meal prep menu, with swaps for dairy-free.

children.text: This makes two 350 ml glasses and takes five minutes.
What you need
2 large handfuls of baby spinach
1 ripe banana
60 g rolled oats
200 g Greek yoghurt
Juice of half a lemon
1 tablespoon chia seeds
200 ml cold water
Method
Blend everything for about 45 seconds until smooth. Add water a splash at a time if it is too thick. Drink it fresh or keep it in the fridge for a day.
Swaps
Use a plain soy yoghurt for a dairy-free version. Swap oats for 30 g of ground almonds if you need to avoid gluten, and skip this if you have a nut allergy.
